To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the amino acid sequence of the HA1 protein of the influenza A (H1N1) virus isolated in mammalian cells is the same as that of the virus that was circulating in the community.

the amino acid sequences of the HA1 proteins of influenza A (subtypes H3N2, H1N1) virus strains isolated from clinical samples and grown in a wide range of mammalian cell types are identical to those of the viruses isolated directly from the clinical specimens.

the HA of influenza A viruses isolated in mammalian and avain cells is identical to that of virus present in the patient from whom the viruses were isolated, and the HA of influenza viruses isolated in primary chick kidney cells and subsequently passaged in eggs is not antigenically identical to the HA of virus present in patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular biology and immunology of influenza virus and the development of new influenza virus vaccines.
the molecular biology of influenza virus and in particular with the genetic basis for host cell adaptation.
the isolation and characterization of influenza viruses from human clinical samples.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the amino acid sequence of the haemagglutinins of influenza A (Aichi/2/68) viruses isolated in MDCK cells, LLC-MK2 cells, guinea-pig and primary chick kidney cell culture, and in the human lung continuous cell culture (MRC- 5), is identical to that of viruses present in the infected human.
the HA1 of H3N 2 viruses isolated in mammalian and avain cell culture are identical to that of viruses isolated in the infected individual.
all mammalian cells tested to date do not impose a selective pressure for amino acid sequence variation in HA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for the influenza A (H1N1) virus, the amino acid sequence of the HA of viruses grown in MDCK cells was the same as that of the virus in the infected patient; however, for influenza A (H2N2) viruses the sequence of the HA grown in MDCK cell culture was different from that of the virus grown in the infected individual.
there was little or no evidence of host-mediated sequence variation in the HA of H3N 2 viruses grown in mammal and primary chick kidney cell cultures.
the host cell used in primary isolation does not impose a selective pressure to change the amino acid sequence in the HA1 region of the HA protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the host cell used for isolation and/or propagation of influenza viruses can influence the selection of variants.
primary cell culture is a good model system for the isolation of influenza virus.

the use of primary or continuous mammlian cells in the laboratory isolation of influenza virus does not result in the selection of viruses with amino acids substitutions in the globar head region of the haemagglutin molecule, as occurs when the virus is isolated in the embryonatd egg.
